analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for automated software bots to buy up event tickets and requires ticket websites to stop them.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill in September 2025, but it is still waiting on the Senate calendar with no floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates the 2016 BOTS Act, which outlaws software that automatically scoops up event tickets faster than people can buy them. It makes it illegal to use bots that break through a ticket website's purchase limits, requires ticket sellers to actually build and maintain systems that enforce their own purchase rules, and requires them to report bot incidents to the Federal Trade Commission within 30 days. It also directs the FBI and Justice Department to coordinate with the FTC on cyberattacks against ticket sites. The version approved by the committee is narrower than the one originally introduced: it dropped the new FTC civil penalties and the mandatory site-security safeguard requirements, and added a provision limiting how the FTC can use its own guidance in enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary fans trying to buy tickets at face value. When bots beat humans to tickets and resell them at a markup, fans pay more or miss events entirely. The bill gives ticket sellers a legal duty to enforce their own purchase limits and gives the FTC and law enforcement new tools and reporting duties to go after bot operators.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it a violation to use automated applications that circumvent a ticket website's access controls or security measures to buy tickets against the site's posted purchase rules [S3].

It requires every online ticket seller to establish, maintain, and regularly update technological controls that actually enforce the purchase limits they post, instead of leaving limits unenforced [S3].
Ticket sellers must report known bot circumvention incidents to the FTC within 30 days, and the FTC must share those reports and consumer complaints with state attorneys general [S3].
The FBI, the Attorney General, and state and local law enforcement must coordinate with the FTC to share information about cyberattacks on ticket sellers' purchase-limit systems [S3].
The FTC must publish compliance guidance for ticket sellers and report to Congress within a year on its enforcement record and any limits on its ability to pursue bots [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ticket sellers (such as Ticketmaster and other online ticket issuers) bear the cost of building, maintaining, and updating bot-detection systems and filing incident reports. Professional scalpers and brokers who rely on automated buying software lose their main tool for acquiring large blocks of tickets. Taxpayers fund the FTC's new reporting, guidance, and enforcement work.

drawbacks.text: The committee-approved version is weaker than the bill as introduced: the mandatory administrative, technical, and physical security safeguards, the third-party service provider oversight requirements, the FTC's direct civil action authority, and the civil penalties (at least $10,000 per day plus $1,000 per violation) all appear as deleted text in the reported bill, replaced by a narrower set of duties [S3].

The reported bill adds a provision that FTC guidance on the law confers no rights on anyone and that the FTC may not base an enforcement action on practices inconsistent with its guidance unless they violate the statute, which constrains how the agency can police the market [S3].

Success depends on ticket sellers actually complying and on FTC enforcement priorities, and bot operators continually adapt their software, so the bill does not guarantee fans will win the race for tickets.

Compliance costs fall on ticket sellers of all sizes, and the bill leaves in place the broader pricing and fee practices of the ticketing market that fans also complain about; this bill addresses only automated purchasing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to fans is real but incremental: it attacks the bot-and-scalper pipeline that drives up resale prices, which matters to anyone who has lost a ticket race to automated buyers. The main cost is compliance work for ticket sellers, much of which they arguably should be doing already since they post purchase limits. The honest weakness is that the committee stripped the bill's enforcement teeth, the civil penalties and direct FTC lawsuits, leaving duties that matter only if the FTC and sellers actively enforce them.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved it in September 2025 and it has been sitting on the Senate calendar waiting for floor time since then.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on January 22, 2025, with Senator Ben Ray Lujan as cosponsor, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee [S1].
On April 30, 2025, the Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S5].

On September 2, 2025, the committee reported the bill, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 144, where a bill waits until Senate leadership or unanimous consent brings it to the floor [S1].
No Senate vote on the bill has taken place as of the latest action record [S5].

The reported substitute version drops several provisions from the introduced bill, including FTC civil penalties of at least $10,000 per day per violation, FTC civil action authority, mandatory site-security safeguards, and a public FTC complaint website [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost because the bill has not been voted on. Bot operators and professional scalpers continue operating under current law, and ticket sellers face none of the new duties, so the status quo favors them for now until the Senate acts.

for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill twice and ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment that narrowed the original provisions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with a Democratic cosponsor and cleared a Republican-run committee without recorded opposition; no floor vote has split the chamber yet.

industries.industry: Online ticket sellers (Ticketmaster/Live Nation, SeatGeek, and similar issuers)
industries.note: They must build and maintain bot-blocking controls and report incidents, which costs money, but the FTC and law enforcement help protect their systems and their posted purchase limits gain legal force. Their interest in crushing bots runs alongside fans' interest in fair access, though sellers also face criticism for under-enforcing their own rules.

Automated ticket-buying software that circumvents purchase controls becomes illegal, and incidents must be reported to the FTC. Their business model depends on beating ordinary buyers to tickets and reselling at a markup.
Enforcement against bots shrinks the supply of cheaply acquired inventory that flows to the secondary market, though resale platforms themselves are not directly regulated by this bill.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Senate calendar, which means it needs either floor time from leadership or agreement to pass by unanimous consent. Uncontroversial consumer bills with bipartisan sponsorship sometimes clear the Senate this way, but many never do; months have passed since it was calendared with no vote. If it passes the Senate, it would still need House action before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
